name: Opus 5 vol regime
strategy: Stagflationary vol-dispersion book: long the physical oil/commodity supply shock (XLE, COMT), short the most rate-and-margin-sensitive equity cohort (IWM), VIX tail closed after FOMC, 45% cash at 4% - low net exposure, high internal dispersion.
reassessment_note: Research (WebSearch/WebFetch, mostly broker and market-wrap sources; I could not find an Oct 30 closing wrap) confirms the regime the book is built on. The Fed held at 3.75-4.00% on Oct 28 in a 10-2 vote with Cook and Hammack dissenting for a hike, upgraded growth to 'strong', and said inflation 'remains elevated'. Futures put about 85% odds on a 25bp hike on Dec 9, the 10-year traded above 5.0% and the curve steepened. The US-Iran war is still constraining Hormuz flows: Brent was about $117 on Oct 23, fell more than 6% on Oct 26, and WTI rebounded about 2.9% to roughly $103 on Fed day. That is a stagflationary mix (high oil, high long yields, a hawkish Fed), which is the case for long energy and commodities against short small caps, so the three core legs stay at their current size. The one change is VIXY. Its stated purpose was a tail into FOMC; that event passed without a shock (VIX about 17), and VIXY loses value to futures contango every week it is held. I take its +4.8% gain and move the 8% to cash, which leaves the book at about 19% net long, with dispersion rather than a decaying volatility product carrying the risk. The short IWM leg serves as the crash hedge if Iran headlines escalate. If a new catalyst appears (Dec 9 FOMC, Hormuz escalation), I will reconsider a volatility tail then.

positions.thesis: This is the core supply-shock leg and stays at 25%. Hormuz disruption from the Iran war has kept crude in roughly the $100-117 range: Brent was about $117 on Oct 23 and WTI about $103 on Oct 28. Integrated majors and E&Ps earn cash at those prices, and XLE's +0.55% leg P&L shows it held up through the Oct 26 Brent drop of more than 6%. A 10% stop caps the loss if a ceasefire collapses the crude risk premium.

This is broad commodity-futures exposure (energy-heavy, plus metals and ags), so the supply-shock thesis does not rest only on equity multiples. Commodity futures also cover inflation persistence, which the Fed itself flagged ('inflation remains elevated'). The leg is down only -0.72% after a sharp Brent pullback. 12% keeps it below XLE because the futures roll costs carry. A 10% stop applies.

Small caps carry the most floating-rate debt and are the most exposed to input costs, which makes them the weakest cohort when the 10-year is above 5%, the Fed is pricing about 85% odds of a December hike, and oil is near $100. This leg funds the long commodity exposure and is now the book's crash hedge as well, after VIXY is closed. The leg is down only -0.84% so far. An 8% stop limits a squeeze if the Fed turns dovish or a ceasefire sparks a risk-on rally.
